# Use of AI before the Federal Labor Arbitration Court (LFTSE, arts. 123 Bis to 123 Quinquies)

**What it is.** Adds a new Chapter I Bis to Title Seven of the Federal Law for State Workers (Ley Federal de los Trabajadores al Servicio del Estado) to regulate the use of AI tools in proceedings before the Federal Labor Arbitration Court.

**Who.** Sen. Agustín Dorantes Lámbarri (PAN). **When.** Presented before the Standing Commission (Comisión Permanente) on July 8, 2026. **Status.** Referred to the Joint Commissions on Justice; Analysis, Monitoring and Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence in Mexico; and Legislative Studies, Second.

## The Guiding Principles

Subjects the use of artificial intelligence tools to ten guiding principles: legality, transparency, traceability, human oversight, explainability, personal data protection, non-discrimination, accountability, proportionality, and information security. Responsibility for actions and rulings remains with judicial officers and public servants with jurisdictional functions: **AI cannot substitute for legal reasoning, automatically assess evidence, determine contested facts, or make decisions without human intervention.**

## Why It Matters

It is one of **14 companion bills** that Senator Dorantes introduced on July 8, 2026 to insert the same chapter, "On the Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools," across nearly all Mexican procedural law—from administrative litigation and labor law to criminal, commercial, agrarian, and military law—as well as a reform to Article 17 of the Constitution. Collectively they seek a single standard: AI as an auxiliary tool, under human oversight and without substituting for the judgment of whoever judges or decides.

# Use of artificial intelligence in amparo proceedings: the Dorantes initiative

**What it is.** An initiative that amends the Ley de Amparo (Amparo Law) to add Chapter I Bis, "On the use of artificial intelligence tools," comprising articles 4 Bis, 4 Ter, 4 Quáter, and 4 Quinquies.

**Who.** Senator Agustín Dorantes Lámbarri (PAN).

**When.** Presented to the Comisión Permanente (Permanent Commission) on July 8, 2026 (signed June 30).

**Status.** Referred to the Joint Commissions on Justice; Analysis, Monitoring, and Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence in Mexico; and Legislative Studies, Second Section.

## What it proposes

The initiative neither prohibits nor mandates: it **permits** the use of AI tools in amparo proceedings, but conditions that use on ten guiding principles—legality, transparency, traceability, human oversight, explainability, personal data protection, non-discrimination, accountability, proportionality, and information security.

The core principle is a clear boundary: **responsibility for every action or ruling remains with the judge.** AI cannot substitute for legal reasoning, automatically assess evidence, determine disputed facts, or make decisions without human intervention.

To maintain a record, it creates a **certificate of artificial intelligence use**—a form to be issued by the Órgano de Administración Judicial (Judicial Administration Body) within no more than 30 business days in its respective jurisdiction.

## Why it matters

It is the amparo component of a **package of 14 mirror initiatives** presented by the same senator that day, introducing the identical chapter into most areas of Mexican procedural law—from administrative litigation and labor law to criminal, commercial, agrarian, and military law—plus a constitutional reform to Article 17.

And it does not arrive in a vacuum. In January 2026 the Poder Judicial (Judiciary) had already recognized, through **jurisprudence** (II.2o.C. J/1 K, registro digital/digital registry 2031639), that AI may be deployed as an auxiliary tool for calculations within amparo proceedings, always subject to human oversight and without replacing the core of judicial reasoning. The Dorantes initiative proposes to codify what the courts already validated through precedent: **AI as support, never as a substitute for judicial judgment.**

# Bill to Protect Dubbing Actors Against Unauthorized Use of Their Voices by Artificial Intelligence

**Claudia Curiel de Icaza (Secretariat of Culture) (other)** · Chamber of Deputies · February 12, 2026 · filed

Government bill seeking to protect dubbing actors against unauthorized use of their voices by Artificial Intelligence, described as the first initiative that would provide protection to workers who lack formal employment contracts, focusing on protecting their primary work tool, which is their voice.

## Topics

- labor rights
- intellectual property

## Observatory Analysis

The reform protects performing artists against voice and image cloning with AI—a real advance—but at a little-discussed cost. In Mexico, image protection was built on the Ley Federal del Derecho de Autor (Federal Law on Copyright), and its article 87 functioned as a general safeguard: jurisprudence 166/2023 (Arjona case, Amparo Directo 7/2022 – Mexican constitutional relief proceeding) had extended it to any person. By reformulating article 87 around the figure of the "performing artist or performer," the new wording could leave someone who is not an artist with less protection against unauthorized use of their image than before the reform. The Observatory documents this tension—progress for some, possible regression for others—as a case study of how AI is legislated in Mexico.

# Oaxaca Penal Code Reform - Chapter X 'Artificial Intelligence' (4-8 years)

**Oaxaca State Congress (Multiparty)** · Oaxaca State Congress · December 4, 2025 · approved

Historic reform to the Código Penal de Oaxaca (Oaxaca Penal Code) approved by the LXVI Legislature on December 2, 2025. Oaxaca becomes one of the first Mexican states to add a specific chapter on AI (Chapter X 'Artificial Intelligence') within Title Four 'Complementary Punishments'. Creates Article 72 Bis establishing enhanced penalties when AI is used as a means to commit any crime defined in the code. Amends paragraph four of Article 249 (Crimes Against Sexual Privacy) to penalize anyone who uses AI to create or distribute manipulated intimate content without consent through deepfakes, images, false audio or video. Penalties: 4 to 8 years imprisonment plus fines of 1,000 to 2,000 UMA (Monthly Adjustment Units—approximately 115,000 to 230,000 pesos). Ex officio prosecution (persecución de oficio). Penalizes exposure, distribution, exhibition, reproduction, transmission, commercialization or exchange by any technological means. Approved with 31 votes in ordinary session. Represents a pioneering structural approach by creating a chapter dedicated exclusively to AI in Mexican state penal code.

- security
- deepfakes
- gender-based violence

# Campeche State Initiative - Digital Violence and AI-Generated Deepfakes (Ley Olimpia + AI)

**Morena Parliamentary Group (16 deputies)** · Campeche State Congress · February 10, 2025 · archived

Initiative INI078LXV0225 presented on February 11, 2025 by the Morena Parliamentary Group (16 deputies) in the LXV Legislature of the Campeche State Congress. Amends Articles 175 Bis, 255, and 260 of the Código Penal de Campeche (Campeche Penal Code) to criminalize digital violence and AI-generated deepfakes within the framework of the Ley Olimpia (Olimpia Law). Article 175 Bis: Imposes 3 to 6 years imprisonment plus a fine of 500 to 1,000 UMA (units of measurement and adjustment) for creating or disseminating sexually explicit or lascivious content via AI using facial data collection or reconstruction of physical features without consent. Article 255: Imposes 3 months to 2 years imprisonment for pornographic content created using AI based on biometric data. Article 260: Imposes 5 to 10 years imprisonment plus a fine of 400 to 800 UMA for the production of child sexual abuse material using facial recognition AI. Citing Sensity AI data: 90-95% of pornographic deepfakes target women. Historic expansion of the Ley Olimpia (Olimpia Law) to include deepfakes and AI-generated content.

# Quintana Roo Penal Code Reform - Art. 20 Bis general aggravating factor for AI (+50% sentence)

**Congreso del Estado de Quintana Roo (Quintana Roo State Congress)** · Congreso del Estado de Quintana Roo · April 14, 2024 · published

Amendment to the Código Penal de Quintana Roo (Quintana Roo Penal Code) that adds Article 20 Bis as a general aggravating factor: increases sentences up to 1.5 times (by half) for ANY crime committed with the use of artificial intelligence. General aggravating factor model versus specific criminal statutes, applicable to current and future crimes. Approved in April 2024, it was challenged through an acción de inconstitucionalidad (constitutional challenge) 104/2024. The Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación (Mexican Supreme Court of Justice, SCJN) upheld its constitutionality on April 28, 2025, establishing the first judicial constitutional precedent on AI regulation in Mexican penal code. The SCJN (Pleno, April 28, 2025) dismissed 5-4 the constitutional challenge against Article 20 Bis; the norm survives and remains in force.

# Amendment to Articles 20 Ter and 20 Quáter of the Ley General de Acceso de las Mujeres a una Vida Libre de Violencia (General Law on Women's Access to a Life Free of Violence)

**Julieta Kristal Vences Valencia (Morena)** · Chamber of Deputies · March 31, 2024 · approved

Initiative presented by Deputy Julieta Kristal Vences Valencia (Morena) to the LXV Legislature on February 18, 2025. Amends and supplements Articles 20 Ter and 20 Quáter of the Ley General de Acceso de las Mujeres a una Vida Libre de Violencia to recognize and punish "digital contract killing" as a new form of digital violence. Classifies as digital violence any action involving manipulation, alteration, or dissemination of images, audio, or video generated through information technologies, generative artificial intelligence tools, or any digital medium with the purpose of harming the dignity, reputation, or safety of women, adolescents, and girls. Responds to documented cases of deepfakes, AI-manipulated content, and misinformation used to discredit women politicians and public figures. Seeks to close legal loopholes that enable impunity in digital political violence and ensure effective protection against new forms of technological aggression toward women. Includes strengthened coordination among education, technology, and security authorities. Unanimously approved by the Committee on Gender Equality in November 2025, pending final vote in the Plenary.
